newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Big powers near pact to cut infotechnology tariffs.
newsitem.headline: Big powers near pact to cut infotechnology tariffs.

text.p: The world's four biggest trading powers appeared on Wednesday to be nearing an agreement to scrap tariffs in the fast-growing information technology sector.

The Big Four -- the United States, the European Union, Japan and Canada -- see an infotech agreement as vital to the success of this week's gathering of the 128-nation World Trade Organisation (WTO) in Singapore.
They see such an accord as freeing up trade in the $600 billion global market for computers, chips and other high-technology products by the year 2000.

All four held meetings on the sidelines of the WTO ministerial conference to settle differences over the Information Technology Agreement (ITA) before trying to persuade other countries to sign up to a deal.
"There is not an agreement yet," European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said after meeting Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky.
"There is agreement on many points. There are some outstanding ones. We are trying to resolve those."
Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda said he hoped there would be an infotech agreement at the Singapore conference.
"I cannot say for sure, but we have been able to get more progress than originally thought," he said. "I think something is possible."

A senior Japanese official said the Big Four, called the Quadrilateral Group, hoped to settle their differences, in particular over the touchy question of which products to include in the deal, by early on Thursday.
He said the four had now agreed an outline framework and were merely filling in details.

"Some legal and technical aspects have to be elaborated," said Yoshiji Nogami, head of economic affairs at Japan's Foreign Ministry. "There is no airtight agreement yet, but we are now in a position to present a Quad position."
Another Japanese official said the Quad's framework agreement proposed information technology tariffs should begin to be reduced in 1997 and be eliminated by 2000.
"On the upstream products and the middle stream products, we can OK (it). We will have zero tariffs by the year 2000," he said. "We can live with that with some sort of flexibility."
Singapore welcomed the draft proposal, saying it would support the ITA initiative.
"We stand ready to join the ITA and look forward to achieving the maximum outcome possible by the end of this meeting," Singapore Minister for Communications Mah Bow Tan told a conference session.

Developing countries have been shown a draft of an ITA worked out by the Quad, but it did not say which products would be included or what sort of flexibility could be granted to developing countries on the timing of the tariff cuts, a Japanese source said.

Indonesian Trade and Industry Minister Tunky Ariwibowo told a news conference the bulk of the proposals contained in the draft outline would be acceptable but Jakarta had problems with some of the products detailed in the ITA.
These were mainly in what he called the "downstream area", meaning lower technology.
Washington hopes that in addition to a broad infotech pact by as many countries as possible, the WTO will endorse the ITA deal in its Ministerial Declaration on Friday.
That would allow WTO members unable to sign on now to do so at a later date by presenting revised tariff schedules at the WTO in Geneva, the U.S. official said.
